analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic makers to delay cheaper competing drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have outlawed 'pay-for-delay' settlements that keep low-cost generics off the market, died in House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes settle patent lawsuits by paying generic competitors to stay off the market for years. The bill would have made those payments illegal under antitrust law, required drug company executives to certify under penalty of perjury that all settlement agreements were disclosed to regulators, and stripped a generic maker of its 180-day marketing exclusivity if it joined such a deal. It was referred to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, employers, and insurers who pay for prescriptions. The bill's own findings note generics cost about 63 percent less than brand-name drugs and account for 56 percent of prescriptions but only 13 percent of drug spending, so faster generic entry lowers drug bills across the board.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and employers who pay drug bills

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful, under the Clayton Act, for a brand-name drug maker to be party to a patent settlement in which a generic applicant receives anything of value and agrees not to market the generic for any period of time [S3].

The bill's findings cite FTC determinations that more than two-thirds of roughly ten settlements in 2006 included a payment from a brand-name maker in exchange for a promise to delay generic entry [S3].

It requires the CEO or negotiating official to certify under penalty of perjury that filings with the FTC and Justice Department are complete, final, and exclusive, closing a loophole for undisclosed side deals [S3].
It strips a generic maker of its 180-day exclusivity period if a court or the FTC finds it violated the new prohibition, removing the incentive to sign a delay deal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, which would lose a tool for extending patent monopolies beyond their expiration, and generic makers who accept such payments, which would lose the compensation but gain earlier market entry instead.

drawbacks.text: Brand manufacturers argue that settling patent disputes is legitimate: a settlement that pays a generic to enter before patent expiration (an 'authorized generic' entry date) is expressly permitted under the bill, and companies contend some patents are valid and deserve defense rather than forced surrender [S3].

Critics of a flat ban note that not every settlement payment is anticompetitive; a blanket rule could push parties into costlier litigation, and the bill would have required litigation to run its course even where the patent is weak.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and broad: generics cost roughly 63 percent less than brand-name drugs, and delay agreements directly postpone that savings, sometimes for years. The cost falls on a concentrated industry and on generic firms that currently collect compensation instead of competing. The main design risk is that the permitted settlement category could be stretched in practice, which is why the disclosure certification and exclusivity forfeiture provisions matter. Weighing it, the public benefit of faster generic competition substantially outweighs the cost to the industry's settlement leverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, and neither one ever took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Henry Waxman introduced the bill on March 9, 2007 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
Three days later it went to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it stayed [S5].
No markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers benefited, since pay-for-delay settlements remained lawful and the generics kept off the market continued to cost consumers full brand prices.

for.name: Henry A. Waxman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited one cosponsor; no committee action followed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to a subcommittee; never held a markup or advanced it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no record of partisan voting exists.

industries.note: The bill would outlaw their practice of paying generic competitors to stay off the market, ending a way to extend monopoly pricing past a patent's practical life. Consumers currently pay brand-name prices during those delays.

Generic makers would lose the option of collecting a settlement payment in exchange for staying off the market, but those that choose to compete could enter and sell earlier instead. First filers would risk forfeiting their 180-day exclusivity if they sign a violating deal.
Faster generic entry means lower prescription costs; the bill's findings note generics cost about 63 percent less than brand-name drugs.
